_note: Each case runs one skill against a fresh copy of examples/fixture-os and then reads the filesystem. Assertions are deliberately structural -- what got written, where, and what stayed untouched -- because that is what the cross-cutting rules actually claim. Two checks run on every case regardless: raw/ stays append-only, and a usage/log.md row gets appended. The frame answers a skill's clarifying question rather than stopping at it: two cases in the first full run wrote nothing at all because corp-os-intake and corp-os-brief correctly refused to proceed without a person -- intake asks when a type is ambiguous, brief asks for a window when meta.json holds no prior brief. Both were doing exactly what their skill says. Reading that as failure would have 'fixed' two skills that were right; the harness was wrong. Cases carry an optional `fixture` -- examples/fixture-os is the shipped default shape, examples/fixture-register is a jobs-off OS with renamed vocabulary and a hand-maintained source layer. The irreversible-path cases run against the register fixture because that is where a role mistake actually costs something.

cases._note:
The only case that starts from an empty directory, and the only one that has not been made to pass. Six runs across three configurations -- the scaffolder unmentioned, the scaffolder called in Step 3, the scaffolder as Step 0 before any question -- all produced a domain-shaped folder (agreements/, renewals.md, vendors/, a template, a clause checklist) and none of the five invariants. 2/9 to 3/10 every time.

Two readings, and they are worth separating before anyone 'fixes' this again. It may be the skill: with no existing OS to anchor to and a request dense with domain content, the structure loses to the vocabulary. Or it may be this harness: the frame says 'the skill is at <path>, read it and follow it', which a model may treat as reference material rather than as the procedure it must execute. Fifteen of sixteen cases follow their skill closely, which argues for the first reading -- but every one of those fifteen starts from an existing OS, so none of them tests what this one tests.

The way to tell them apart is to install the plugin and run /corp-os in a real session against an empty folder. Until that is done, this is recorded as unresolved rather than patched again.

cases.prompt: Build me a stakeholder map for the renewal — who's involved and where each of them stands.
cases._note:
Third version of this case's assertion, and the first two were both wrong about the skill rather than the reverse.

v1 asserted the string 'corp-os-configure' appeared in the answer. It failed a run that declared people/ with role, entry_schema, index_line, label_field, order_by and decay, behind a written proposal citing gate.mode -- it simply never said the skill's name. Testing vocabulary, not behavior.

v2 asserted config.json changed. Two live runs took two different legitimate paths: one declared the layer and filed entries, one wrote the proposal and built the map from what already existed, leaving the declaration for the person to confirm. Asserting config.json changed picks a winner between two correct behaviors.

What both correct runs did, and what improvising a layer inline does not, is leave a proposal behind. That plus the incomplete-index check covers the failure this case exists for: a layer conjured to serve a rendering, with no review and the wrong shape.

Measured, and left failing on purpose: 2/5 runs across three rounds. One declared the layer with full shape and filed a proposal; one filed the proposal and built the view from what already existed; three built the view and mentioned the gap only in the answer, where it died with the session. A wording pass making the proposal requirement explicit was tried and measured at 0/2, so it was reverted rather than kept -- prose that does not move the number is churn, and this repo has argued that four times about other people's code. Nothing mechanical catches this one: the runs that miss it leave no dangling reference and no undeclared directory, because they infer the view from layers that do exist. Deciding a layer is warranted is judgment, which is the one thing the shipped scripts cannot take over. Recorded as an open number rather than patched a third time.

file_lacks.why: build_index.py renders this banner for any layer declared without an index_line, and lists its entries as bare links. It is the exact machine-visible signature of a layer declared without the configure interrogation -- the shape mistake this check exists to catch, made once already in this repo

expect_added.why: a layer is a structural change to what the OS can hold, and the gate is what stops one being shaped wrong in passing. The proposal is the artifact that survives the session; a run that quietly invents a directory to render a panel leaves nothing to review

cases._note:
Second version. The first described the material in the prompt instead of staging it, then asserted raw files would be written — incoherent, because there was nothing on disk to file, and it failed 0/2 for that reason rather than any of the skill's. The material now lives in fixture-os/_incoming/, which the generator ignores because of the leading underscore.

The first version also checked the answer for the string 'retriev', which is the vocabulary mistake this suite has now made three times — a run can distinguish the two populations perfectly while saying 'fetchable' or 'still have access to'. What replaced it is the calendar log, which has to be declined, named with the material's own word.

The expect_untouched on claims/ stays as the assertion most likely to be wrong: Step 4 says mint in batches through the gate, so a run that goes on to mint with a proposal is also defensible. If it fails that way, the check changes and the reason gets written here.

Third version, and the flagged assertion was the one that broke. expect_untouched on claims/ encoded 'a first pass files source and stops', which the skill does not say — Step 4 says mint in batches through the gate. Both runs did exactly that: they filed source, then minted with a proposal, and the universal gate check passed on both. The rule I asserted was stricter than the rule that exists, which is the seventh time an assertion in this suite has been wrong about a skill rather than the reverse. Replaced with the property that actually matters at a migration's scale: the batch left a persisted proposal behind.

cases._note:
fixture-register is the right target precisely because the pattern cannot bind there: jobs is disabled and the vocabulary is renamed. Two things are being tested at once — that the claims requirement binds anyway despite claim being renamed to entry, which is the portability thesis, and that the jobs requirement refuses out loud rather than degrading into an empty panel.

Deliberately not asserting that config.json is untouched: declaring the missing layer through corp-os-configure is one of the two legitimate answers, and asserting against it would test the frame rather than the skill. That mistake has been made seven times in this suite.

Second version. The first asserted nothing under patterns/ was touched at all, and it failed at 50% because a run added patterns/pack.json — recording which pack and version the OS is on, which is Step 4 of the skill in as many words. The check forbade what the skill instructs. Eighth time in this suite that an assertion has been wrong about a skill rather than the reverse.

expect_unmodified on the teammate's file is the right shape: it catches editing theirs to fit, which is the real failure, and permits adding a local file, which is forking visibly rather than silently.

expect_unmodified.name: the teammate's pattern was not edited to make it bind
expect_unmodified.why: weakening a requirement to make a refusal go away produces an output that renders an empty panel, which reads as a state rather than a defect. Editing an adopted pattern also forks the pack silently, so the next update reports drift nobody chose
